content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published comprehensive guidelines on person-centered strategic information for viral hepatitis. These guidelines aim to assist countries in scaling up prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services for hepatitis. The document emphasizes the use of data to support national efforts in combating hepatitis B and C, focusing on person-centered health services and core interventions. The guidelines outline a monitoring and evaluation framework that includes ten core indicators, organized along the results chain from inputs to impact. This framework is designed to identify programmatic gaps and improve the effectiveness of hepatitis programs. Key indicators include the prevalence of chronic hepatitis B and C, vaccination coverage, testing and treatment rates, and the reduction of new infections and mortality. The WHO highlights the importance of using existing data to strengthen country-level surveillance and planning. Countries are encouraged to validate available data, identify gaps, and use this information for decision-making, investment planning, and scaling up services. Specific recommendations include conducting prevalence surveys, creating person-centered treatment databases, and utilizing drug consumption data to triangulate treatment coverage. The guidelines also stress the integration of hepatitis data into broader health information systems to enhance routine monitoring and analysis. This includes strengthening surveillance of advanced liver diseases and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) to better estimate the impact of hepatitis-related mortality. Globally, hepatitis B and C remain significant public health challenges, with an estimated 254 million people living with chronic hepatitis B and 50 million with chronic hepatitis C as of 2022. Despite progress in reducing perinatal transmission through infant vaccination programs, diagnosis and treatment rates remain low. For example, only 13% of individuals with chronic hepatitis B and 36% with chronic hepatitis C had been diagnosed by the end of 2022, with even fewer receiving treatment. The WHO's global health sector strategy for 2022–2030 aims to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. This strategy focuses on five core interventions: infant hepatitis B vaccination, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, blood and injection safety, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and expanded testing and treatment coverage. The strategy also emphasizes the need for robust data systems to monitor progress and inform decision-making. The guidelines provide a stepwise approach to strengthening surveillance and monitoring systems, with a focus on person-centered care. Countries are encouraged to invest in information systems, integrate hepatitis data into broader health systems, and use data to drive programmatic decisions. By doing so, the WHO aims to support countries in achieving the global targets for hepatitis elimination.
